rationale: This ethnographic study examines rural community resistance and political-cultural conflict over the construction of the El Zapotillo mega-dam in Jalisco, Mexico, focusing on threatened village inundation, forced displacement, and competing ontologies of water and human dignity. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (Criterion 1), last-mile legal/regulatory service-access mechanisms (Criterion 2 narrow), or water/sanitation service-access outcomes (Criterion 4).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Both narrow and plain Criterion 2 readings yield exclude because the study fails Criterion 1 and Criterion 4: although it touches on broad water governance, state infrastructure policy, and rights (satisfying plain Criterion 2), it examines mega-dam construction, village inundation/displacement, and cultural conceptions of water rather than household or community water or sanitation service access outcomes.

evidence_quotes.quote: This article will analyze the social emergency raised in Temacapulín, a small town in Jalisco, Mexico, against the government's desire to build a mega dam to bring water to remote cities, which would mean the disappearance of the village and the displacement of its inhabitants.
The ethnographic work shows that the resistance of the villagers brings to light the existence of different ways of managing water, linked to different conceptions of water itself
The resulting political conflict shows as well how these different positions conceal distinct ideas about where human dignity resides, and what and which are the rights of men and women.
